Lecture 13

Forced systems and left and right eigenvectors

We derive the variation-of-constants formula for linear systems and use it for exponential and constant forcing. We introduce left eigenvectors, normalize them against the right ones, and expand the initial data and the forcing in modes. We show why orthogonal projections do not work for a general matrix and what changes for a defective one.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Derive the variation-of-constants formula for x˙=A(t)x+b(t)\dot{\vv x}=A(t)\vv x+\vv b(t)x˙=A(t)x+b(t) and solve an initial-value problem with it.
  • For a diagonalizable matrix, compute left eigenvectors with ℓi†rj=δij\vv\ell_i^{\adj}\vv r_j=\delta_{ij}ℓi†​rj​=δij​ and expand initial data and forcing in modes.
  • Explain why orthogonal projections onto eigenvectors give the modal coefficients only when the chosen eigenvectors are pairwise orthogonal, which is possible exactly for a normal matrix.
  • Solve a forced two-by-two system with a defective matrix by the exponential eλt(I+tN)\ee^{\lambda t}(I+tN)eλt(I+tN).

Lectures 11 and 12 solved homogeneous linear systems with the propagator. A physical system is usually driven as well: salt is poured into a tank, a force acts on a body. In this lecture we solve the inhomogeneous system x˙=A(t)x+b(t)\dot{\vv x}=A(t)\vv x+\vv b(t)x˙=A(t)x+b(t) by variation of constants, the method of Lectures 5 and 8. For a constant diagonalizable matrix we then split the initial data and the forcing into the shares of the individual modes. These shares are computed with left eigenvectors. Orthogonal projections give them only for special matrices.

13.1 Variation of constants

As in Lectures 10–12, III is the identity matrix and JJJ an open interval of times. Let A(t)A(t)A(t) be an n×nn\times nn×n matrix and b(t)\vv b(t)b(t) a column of nnn functions, all continuous on JJJ, with real or complex values. We solve x˙=A(t)x+b(t),x(t0)=x0,\dot{\vv x}=A(t)\vv x+\vv b(t),\qquad \vv x(t_0)=\vv x_0,x˙=A(t)x+b(t),x(t0​)=x0​,(13.1) with t0∈Jt_0\in Jt0​∈J and x0∈Cn\vv x_0\in\C^nx0​∈Cn. The function b\vv bb is the forcing.

x˙=A(t)x+b(t),x(t0)=x0,\dot{\vv x}=A(t)\vv x+\vv b(t),\qquad \vv x(t_0)=\vv x_0,x˙=A(t)x+b(t),x(t0​)=x0​,(13.1)

Let XXX be a fundamental matrix of the homogeneous system x˙=A(t)x\dot{\vv x}=A(t)\vv xx˙=A(t)x. By Lecture 11 its solutions are X(t)cX(t)\vv cX(t)c with constant vectors c\vv cc. As in Lectures 5 and 8 we replace the constant by a function and try x(t)=X(t)c(t)\vv x(t)=X(t)\vv c(t)x(t)=X(t)c(t). The product rule gives x˙=X˙c+Xc˙=AXc+Xc˙=Ax+Xc˙.\dot{\vv x}=\dot X\vv c+X\dot{\vv c}=A X\vv c+X\dot{\vv c}=A\vv x+X\dot{\vv c}.x˙=X˙c+Xc˙=AXc+Xc˙=Ax+Xc˙. Hence x\vv xx solves the system exactly when X(t)c˙(t)=b(t)X(t)\dot{\vv c}(t)=\vv b(t)X(t)c˙(t)=b(t), that is, c˙=X(t)−1b(t)\dot{\vv c}=X(t)^{-1}\vv b(t)c˙=X(t)−1b(t). Integration from t0t_0t0​, with c(t0)=X(t0)−1x0\vv c(t_0)=X(t_0)^{-1}\vv x_0c(t0​)=X(t0​)−1x0​, gives the formula of the next theorem.

Theorem 13.1 (Variation of constants for systems). Let AAA and b\vv bb be continuous on JJJ, let Φ\PhiΦ be the propagator of x˙=A(t)x\dot{\vv x}=A(t)\vv xx˙=A(t)x, and let t0∈Jt_0\in Jt0​∈J and x0∈Cn\vv x_0\in\C^nx0​∈Cn. The problem (13.1) has exactly one solution on JJJ, namely x(t)=Φ(t,t0)x0+∫t0tΦ(t,τ) b(τ) ⁣dτ.\vv x(t)=\Phi(t,t_0)\vv x_0+\int_{t_0}^t\Phi(t,\tau)\,\vv b(\tau)\dd \tau.x(t)=Φ(t,t0​)x0​+∫t0​t​Φ(t,τ)b(τ)dτ.(13.2) For a constant matrix AAA, x(t)=e(t−t0)Ax0+∫t0te(t−τ)A b(τ) ⁣dτ.\vv x(t)=\ee^{(t-t_0)A}\vv x_0+\int_{t_0}^t\ee^{(t-\tau)A}\,\vv b(\tau)\dd \tau.x(t)=e(t−t0​)Ax0​+∫t0​t​e(t−τ)Ab(τ)dτ.(13.3)

Proof. First, we show that (13.2) is a solution. Let XXX be a fundamental matrix, so that Φ(t,τ)=X(t)X(τ)−1\Phi(t,\tau)=X(t)X(\tau)^{-1}Φ(t,τ)=X(t)X(τ)−1. Then (13.2) reads x(t)=X(t)c(t)\vv x(t)=X(t)\vv c(t)x(t)=X(t)c(t) with c(t)=X(t0)−1x0+∫t0tX(τ)−1b(τ) ⁣dτ.\vv c(t)=X(t_0)^{-1}\vv x_0+\int_{t_0}^tX(\tau)^{-1}\vv b(\tau)\dd \tau.c(t)=X(t0​)−1x0​+∫t0​t​X(τ)−1b(τ)dτ. The determinant of X(τ)X(\tau)X(τ) has no zeros on JJJ by Lecture 11. By the cofactor formula for the inverse (GM 22), the entries of X(τ)−1X(\tau)^{-1}X(τ)−1 are continuous functions of τ\tauτ. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, applied to each entry, c\vv cc is C1C^1C1 with c˙(t)=X(t)−1b(t)\dot{\vv c}(t)=X(t)^{-1}\vv b(t)c˙(t)=X(t)−1b(t). The computation before the theorem then gives x˙=Ax+Xc˙=Ax+b\dot{\vv x}=A\vv x+X\dot{\vv c}=A\vv x+\vv bx˙=Ax+Xc˙=Ax+b. At t=t0t=t_0t=t0​ the integral vanishes, so x(t0)=X(t0)X(t0)−1x0=x0\vv x(t_0)=X(t_0)X(t_0)^{-1}\vv x_0=\vv x_0x(t0​)=X(t0​)X(t0​)−1x0​=x0​.

Next, let y\vv yy be a second solution of (13.1). The difference x−y\vv x-\vv yx−y solves the homogeneous system and vanishes at t0t_0t0​. By uniqueness for the homogeneous system (Lecture 11) it vanishes on JJJ.

Finally, for a constant matrix Φ(t,τ)=e(t−τ)A\Phi(t,\tau)=\ee^{(t-\tau)A}Φ(t,τ)=e(t−τ)A by Lecture 11, and (13.2) becomes (13.3). ■

Formula (13.3) is also called Duhamel’s formula. The first term of (13.2) is the free motion with the given data. The second term is the response to the forcing, and it has zero data at t0t_0t0​. Heuristically, the forcing acting during a short interval [τ,τ+Δτ][\tau,\tau+\Delta \tau][τ,τ+Δτ] changes the state, compared with the motion without this forcing, by about b(τ)Δτ\vv b(\tau)\Delta \taub(τ)Δτ. The propagator carries this change from the time τ\tauτ to the time ttt, and the integral adds these contributions over all earlier times.

13.4 Left and right eigenvectors

Let AAA be a constant matrix with a basis of eigenvectors. By Lecture 11 the solution of the homogeneous system is a sum of modes, and the coefficients come from Pc=x0P\vv c=\vv x_0Pc=x0​. Lecture 10 solved such systems through rows α\vv\alphaα with αA=μα\vv\alpha A=\mu\vv\alphaαA=μα. We now relate the two. Lecture 11 wrote vj\vv v_jvj​ for the eigenvectors. In this lecture they are paired with a second family of vectors, so we write rj\vv r_jrj​ (right) for the eigenvectors and ℓj\vv\ell_jℓj​ (left) for the new vectors.

We use the conjugate transpose A†=A‾TA^{\adj}=\conj A^{\T}A†=AT. For a column u∈Cn\vv u\in\C^nu∈Cn the row u†\vv u^{\adj}u† has the entries uk‾\conj{u_k}uk​​, and u†w=∑k=1nuk‾ wk=⟨u,w⟩\vv u^{\adj}\vv w=\sum_{k=1}^n\conj{u_k}\,w_k=\inner{\vv u}{\vv w}u†w=k=1∑n​uk​​wk​=⟨u,w⟩ is the standard inner product of Cn\C^nCn (LA 7, Definition “Inner product, physics convention”). We also use (BC)†=C†B†(BC)^{\adj}=C^{\adj}B^{\adj}(BC)†=C†B† (LA 9, Proposition “Properties of adjoints”).

Definition 13.5 (Left eigenvector). Let AAA be an n×nn\times nn×n matrix and λ\lambdaλ an eigenvalue of AAA. A nonzero column ℓ∈Cn\vv\ell\in\C^nℓ∈Cn is a left eigenvector of AAA for λ\lambdaλ if A†ℓ=λ‾ ℓ.A^{\adj}\vv\ell=\conj\lambda\,\vv\ell.A†ℓ=λℓ.(13.7) An eigenvector r\vv rr with Ar=λrA\vv r=\lambda\vv rAr=λr is then also called a right eigenvector.

The conjugate transpose of (13.7) is ℓ†A=λ ℓ†.\vv\ell^{\adj}A=\lambda\,\vv\ell^{\adj}.ℓ†A=λℓ†.(13.8) So the row ℓ†\vv\ell^{\adj}ℓ† multiplies AAA from the left and returns a multiple of itself. This is the algebraic row convention: the rows w\vv ww with wA=λw\vv wA=\lambda\vv wwA=λw are exactly the rows ℓ†\vv\ell^{\adj}ℓ†. They are the rows α\vv\alphaα of the linear integrable combinations of Lecture 10, with μ=λ\mu=\lambdaμ=λ.

ℓ†A=λ ℓ†.\vv\ell^{\adj}A=\lambda\,\vv\ell^{\adj}.ℓ†A=λℓ†.(13.8)

For a real matrix and a real eigenvalue, ℓ\vv\ellℓ can be chosen real, because the real singular matrix AT−λIA^{\T}-\lambda IAT−λI has a nonzero real vector in its null space (GM 22). Then ℓ†=ℓT\vv\ell^{\adj}=\vv\ell^{\T}ℓ†=ℓT, and (13.7) reads ATℓ=λℓA^{\T}\vv\ell=\lambda\vv\ellATℓ=λℓ. For a real matrix and a nonreal eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ, the column ℓ\vv\ellℓ is an eigenvector of ATA^{\T}AT for λ‾\conj\lambdaλ, and the row that belongs to λ\lambdaλ is ℓ†\vv\ell^{\adj}ℓ†, not ℓT\vv\ell^{\T}ℓT. The conjugation in (13.7) makes the coefficient ℓ†x\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv xℓ†x an inner product ⟨ℓ,x⟩\inner{\vv\ell}{\vv x}⟨ℓ,x⟩.

Left eigenvectors exist for every eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ. Indeed, a determinant does not change under transposition (GM 22), and the determinant of the complex conjugate matrix is the conjugate of the determinant, since it is a polynomial in the entries with integer coefficients. Hence det⁡(λ‾I−A†)=det⁡(λI−A)‾=0\det(\conj\lambda I-A^{\adj})=\conj{\det(\lambda I-A)}=0det(λI−A†)=det(λI−A)​=0.

Lemma 13.6 (Biorthogonality). Let ℓ\vv\ellℓ be a left eigenvector of AAA for λ\lambdaλ and r\vv rr a right eigenvector for λ′\lambda'λ′. If λ≠λ′\lambda\ne\lambda'λ=λ′, then ℓ†r=0\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv r=0ℓ†r=0.

Proof. We compute ℓ†Ar\vv\ell^{\adj}A\vv rℓ†Ar in two ways. By (13.8) it equals λ ℓ†r\lambda\,\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv rλℓ†r, and by Ar=λ′rA\vv r=\lambda'\vv rAr=λ′r it equals λ′ ℓ†r\lambda'\,\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv rλ′ℓ†r. Hence (λ−λ′) ℓ†r=0(\lambda-\lambda')\,\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv r=0(λ−λ′)ℓ†r=0. ■

Let A=PDP−1A=PDP^{-1}A=PDP−1 as in Lecture 11, with the columns r1,…,rn\vv r_1,\dots,\vv r_nr1​,…,rn​ of PPP and Arj=λjrjA\vv r_j=\lambda_j\vv r_jArj​=λj​rj​. We define ℓj\vv\ell_jℓj​ by the condition that ℓj†\vv\ell_j^{\adj}ℓj†​ is row jjj of P−1P^{-1}P−1.

Proof. First, multiplying A=PDP−1A=PDP^{-1}A=PDP−1 by P−1P^{-1}P−1 from the left gives P−1A=DP−1P^{-1}A=DP^{-1}P−1A=DP−1. 13.5 Orthogonal projections

The coefficients in (13.10) are not the coefficients of the orthogonal projections onto the eigenvectors, except for special matrices. The orthogonal projection of x\vv xx onto the line of rj\vv r_jrj​ is cjrjc_j\vv r_jcj​rj​ with the coefficient cj=rj†xrj†rjc_j=\frac{\vv r_j^{\adj}\vv x}{\vv r_j^{\adj}\vv r_j}cj​=rj†​rj​rj†​x​(13.13) (LA 8, Definition “Orthogonal projection”, with the unit vector rj/rj†rj\vv r_j/\sqrt{\vv r_j^{\adj}\vv r_j}rj​/rj†​rj​​). A matrix AAA is normal if A†A=AA†A^{\adj}A=AA^{\adj}A†A=AA† (LA 9, Definition “Normal operator”). This meaning of the word is unrelated to the normal modes of Lecture 14.

cj=rj†xrj†rjc_j=\frac{\vv r_j^{\adj}\vv x}{\vv r_j^{\adj}\vv r_j}cj​=rj†​rj​rj†​x​(13.13)

Proposition 13.10 (Orthogonal modal projections). Let r1,…,rn\vv r_1,\dots,\vv r_nr1​,…,rn​ be a basis of Cn\C^nCn of eigenvectors of AAA.

  • The identity x=∑jcjrj\vv x=\sum_jc_j\vv r_jx=∑j​cj​rj​, with cjc_jcj​ from (13.13), holds for every x∈Cn\vv x\in\C^nx∈Cn if and only if the rj\vv r_jrj​ are pairwise orthogonal. Then ℓj=rj/(rj†rj)\vv\ell_j=\vv r_j/(\vv r_j^{\adj}\vv r_j)ℓj​=rj​/(rj†​rj​).

  • The matrix AAA has a basis of pairwise orthogonal eigenvectors if and only if AAA is normal.

Proof. First, let the rj\vv r_jrj​ be pairwise orthogonal. Then the vectors ri/(ri†ri)\vv r_i/(\vv r_i^{\adj}\vv r_i)ri​/(ri†​ri​) satisfy (13.9), so they are the ℓi\vv\ell_iℓi​ by the dual-mode proposition, and (13.10) is the claimed identity. Conversely, let the identity hold, and apply it to x=rk\vv x=\vv r_kx=rk​. The coordinates of rk\vv r_krk​ in the basis are δjk\delta_{jk}δjk​, and coordinates in a basis are unique. Hence rj†rk=0\vv r_j^{\adj}\vv r_k=0rj†​rk​=0 for j≠kj\ne kj=k.

Next, dividing pairwise orthogonal eigenvectors by their lengths gives an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. By the complex spectral theorem (LA 10, Theorem “Complex spectral theorem”) such a basis exists if and only if AAA is normal. ■

Self-adjoint matrices, A†=AA^{\adj}=AA†=A, are normal. They include the real symmetric matrices. For a normal matrix an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors exists, and for such a basis ℓj=rj\vv\ell_j=\vv r_jℓj​=rj​. A normal matrix with a repeated eigenvalue also has bases of eigenvectors that are not orthogonal, and for them the orthogonal projections fail. The matrix of the damped oscillator is real, so A†=ATA^{\adj}=A^{\T}A†=AT. It is not normal for γ>0\gamma>0γ>0, because the entries (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) of AATAA^{\T}AAT and ATAA^{\T}AATA are −2γ-2\gamma−2γ and 2γω022\gamma\omega_0^22γω02​. For a matrix that is not normal no choice of eigenvectors makes the orthogonal projections correct, and the left eigenvectors are needed. When the eigenvalues are distinct, each eigenvector is fixed up to a factor, so there is no choice at all.

13.7 Defective matrices

The dual modes need a basis of eigenvectors. A defective matrix has none. For a defective two-by-two matrix, moreover, the left eigenvector cannot be normalized against the right one.

Proposition 13.12 (Defective two-by-two matrices). Let AAA be a defective two-by-two matrix with the double eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ, let r\vv rr be a right and ℓ\vv\ellℓ a left eigenvector. Then ℓ†r=0\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv r=0ℓ†r=0.

Proof. Let N=A−λIN=A-\lambda IN=A−λI. By Lecture 12, N≠0N\ne0N=0, N2=0N^2=0N2=0, and the eigenvectors of AAA are the nonzero vectors of the line ker⁡N\ker NkerN. Every vector NuN\vv uNu lies in ker⁡N\ker NkerN, because N(Nu)=0N(N\vv u)=0N(Nu)=0. Since N≠0N\ne0N=0, some NuN\vv uNu is nonzero, so it is a nonzero multiple of r\vv rr. Hence r=Nu\vv r=N\vv ur=Nu for some u\vv uu. By (13.8), ℓ†N=ℓ†A−λℓ†=0\vv\ell^{\adj}N=\vv\ell^{\adj}A-\lambda\vv\ell^{\adj}=0ℓ†N=ℓ†A−λℓ†=0, so ℓ†r=ℓ†Nu=0\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv r=\vv\ell^{\adj}N\vv u=0ℓ†r=ℓ†Nu=0. ■

A defective matrix has no basis of eigenvectors, so the expansion in modes is not available. For the two-by-two matrix of the proposition, moreover, the coefficient ℓ†x/ℓ†r\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv x/\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv rℓ†x/ℓ†r of the eigenvector would have a zero denominator. The left eigenvector still gives one linear integrable combination z=ℓ†xz=\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv xz=ℓ†x, with z˙=λz+ℓ†b\dot z=\lambda z+\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv bz˙=λz+ℓ†b, as for the matrix (1101)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)(10​11​) of Lecture 10, which has only one linear integrable combination, up to a factor. Summary

The inhomogeneous linear system with continuous coefficients has exactly one solution for each initial value. Variation of constants gives it as the free motion plus the propagated forcing, x(t)=Φ(t,t0)x0+∫t0tΦ(t,τ)b(τ) ⁣dτ\vv x(t)=\Phi(t,t_0)\vv x_0+\int_{t_0}^t\Phi(t,\tau)\vv b(\tau)\dd \taux(t)=Φ(t,t0​)x0​+∫t0​t​Φ(t,τ)b(τ)dτ. For a second-order scalar equation the upper right entry of the propagator is the kernel of Lecture 8. For a constant matrix and the forcing eσtb0\ee^{\sigma t}\vv b_0eσtb0​, with σ\sigmaσ not an eigenvalue, a particular solution is eσt(σI−A)−1b0\ee^{\sigma t}(\sigma I-A)^{-1}\vv b_0eσt(σI−A)−1b0​. For a diagonalizable matrix the left eigenvectors, normalized by ℓi†rj=δij\vv\ell_i^{\adj}\vv r_j=\delta_{ij}ℓi†​rj​=δij​, give the share of the data and of the forcing in each mode. Orthogonal projections give these shares only when the chosen eigenvectors are pairwise orthogonal, which is possible exactly for a normal matrix. A defective two-by-two matrix has ℓ†r=0\vv\ell^{\adj}\vv r=0ℓ†r=0, and the forced system is solved with eλt(I+tN)\ee^{\lambda t}(I+tN)eλt(I+tN).

  • Variation of constants: x(t)=Φ(t,t0)x0+∫t0tΦ(t,τ)b(τ) ⁣dτ\vv x(t)=\Phi(t,t_0)\vv x_0+\int_{t_0}^t\Phi(t,\tau)\vv b(\tau)\dd \taux(t)=Φ(t,t0​)x0​+∫t0​t​Φ(t,τ)b(τ)dτ; for constant AAA, Φ(t,τ)=e(t−τ)A\Phi(t,\tau)=\ee^{(t-\tau)A}Φ(t,τ)=e(t−τ)A.

  • Exponential forcing: if σ\sigmaσ is not an eigenvalue of AAA, then eσt(σI−A)−1b0\ee^{\sigma t}(\sigma I-A)^{-1}\vv b_0eσt(σI−A)−1b0​ solves x˙=Ax+eσtb0\dot{\vv x}=A\vv x+\ee^{\sigma t}\vv b_0x˙=Ax+eσtb0​.

  • Left eigenvector: A†ℓ=λ‾ℓA^{\adj}\vv\ell=\conj\lambda\vv\ellA†ℓ=λℓ, equivalently ℓ†A=λℓ†\vv\ell^{\adj}A=\lambda\vv\ell^{\adj}ℓ†A=λℓ†; for diagonalizable AAA, ℓi†rj=δij\vv\ell_i^{\adj}\vv r_j=\delta_{ij}ℓi†​rj​=δij​, x=∑j(ℓj†x)rj\vv x=\sum_j(\vv\ell_j^{\adj}\vv x)\vv r_jx=∑j​(ℓj†​x)rj​ and etA=∑jeλjtrjℓj†\ee^{tA}=\sum_j\ee^{\lambda_jt}\vv r_j\vv\ell_j^{\adj}etA=∑j​eλj​trj​ℓj†​.

  • Normal matrices: orthogonal projections onto eigenvectors give the modal coefficients if and only if the chosen eigenvectors are pairwise orthogonal, which is possible exactly when A†A=AA†A^{\adj}A=AA^{\adj}A†A=AA†.

Lecture 14 applies modes to coupled oscillators. Their mass and stiffness matrices are symmetric, and the modes are orthogonal in a product weighted by the masses.

Reading: Riley, Hobson and Bence, Mathematical Methods for Physics and Engineering, 3rd ed., §8.12.7 and §8.13.1 (normal matrices and their eigenvectors) and §8.13.4 (eigenvectors of a general square matrix). Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, AMS, 2012, §3.2 (formula (3.48), Duhamel’s formula) and §3.4 (Theorem 3.12, the inhomogeneous system); Teschl writes Π\PiΠ for the propagator and ggg for the forcing.
